pointers.sentence: A Content Security Policy tells the browser which scripts, styles and images a page may load; the 6.0 notes give it as a defence against content injection such as cross-site scripting (`docs/releases/6.0.txt`).
Each maps a directive to its sources and is empty by default, which writes no header (`django/conf/global_settings.py`).

The enumeration `CSP` names the two headers, the specification's quoted keywords such as `CSP.SELF`, and one placeholder of Django's own, `CSP.NONCE`, which stands in a policy for the request's nonce (`django/utils/csp.py:CSP`).

`ContentSecurityPolicyMiddleware` gives each request a `LazyNonce`, made only when first read, on the way in, and on the way out writes each header whose policy is not empty and which the response lacks (`django/middleware/csp.py:ContentSecurityPolicyMiddleware`).
The context processor `django.template.context_processors.csp` gives a template the nonce as `"csp_nonce"` (`django/template/context_processors.py:csp`).
The function `build_policy` puts the nonce in place of the placeholder if something read it, and otherwise drops the placeholder (`django/utils/csp.py:build_policy`).

The decorators `csp_override` and `csp_report_only_override` give one view a policy that replaces the setting's entirely; an empty one leaves that header off (`django/views/decorators/csp.py:_make_csp_decorator`).
A new project has no policy: the settings startproject writes name neither the middleware nor the processor (`django/conf/project_template/project_name/settings.py-tpl`).

Without an argument, `{% csp_nonce_attr %}` writes `nonce="…"` from the context's `"csp_nonce"`, or nothing when the context has none; given a form's media, it writes the media's tags, with the nonce if any (`django/utils/csp.py:nonce_attr`; [The built-in tags](../templates/tags.md)).
Since 6.1 the admin's templates, admindocs' and the CSRF failure page carry it on their `<script>`, `<style>` and `<link>` elements (`docs/releases/6.1.txt`).

Django's own failure page does not: when the project has no `"403_csrf.html"`, the view `csrf_failure` renders the built-in `"csrf_403.html"` with an `Engine` of its own, and adds the nonce itself (`django/views/csrf.py:csrf_failure`).
Under 6.0.8 the page's inline style had no nonce, so a browser would refuse it (`docs/ref/csp.txt`).
It is registered without `deploy=True`, so check reports it without --deploy (`django/core/checks/security/base.py:check_csp_nonce_context_processor`; [The security checks](../security/checks.md)).

Until 5.2.15 and 6.0.6 that salt was the cookie's name followed by the caller's salt, so the cookie "draft" with the salt "s" and the cookie "drafts" with none made the same one, and a value signed for either was accepted for the other (CVE-2026-6873, `docs/releases/5.2.15.txt`; [Security fixes: disclosure, spoofing and privilege](security-fixes-exposure.md)).

`HttpResponseBase.set_signed_cookie` has since signed with a salt of a fixed prefix, the length of the caller's salt, that salt and the name, so that no two pairs make one string (`django/core/signing.py:_cookie_signer_salt`).

For the cookies signed before, the function `_unsign_cookie` tries the old salt when the new one fails for any reason but age, if `SIGNED_COOKIE_LEGACY_SALT_FALLBACK` is true (`django/core/signing.py:_unsign_cookie`).

The 6.1 notes list "Signed cookies now use an unambiguous salt derivation by default" among its features (`docs/releases/6.1.txt`), but 5.2.17 and 6.0.8 already sign with the new salt: what 6.1 changed is what is read.

Since 6.1, at the default, a project's own cookies signed before the fix are refused too, under every name and salt: what `set_signed_cookie("draft", "4", salt="s")` wrote then was signed with the same old salt, "drafts" (`django/core/signing.py:_cookie_signer_legacy_salt`).
6.1.1 and this commit warn when a project sets the fallback, to either value (`django/conf/__init__.py:Settings.__init__`).

Nothing warns when an old cookie is refused: from 6.1, at the default, `HttpRequest.get_signed_cookie` raises `BadSignature` for it, or returns the default it was given, as for a forged one (`django/http/request.py:HttpRequest.get_signed_cookie`).

6.1 deprecated SHA-1 as the default algorithm of `salted_hmac`, the keyed hash under Django's signing ([What changed](../changes.md#an-old-habit-release-by-release)), and of `base64_hmac`, with which `Signer` signs: under 5.2.17 and 6.0.8 `base64_hmac("journal", "entry", "journal-key")` returns its digest without a word, and 6.1.1 and this commit return the same digest and warn (`django/core/signing.py:base64_hmac`).

Django's own callers name the algorithm, `Signer` the one it was made with, SHA-256 by default, so signing never meets the warning (`django/core/signing.py:Signer.signature`; [Secret keys and `django.utils.crypto`](../security/keys.md), [Signing: `Signer`, `TimestampSigner`, `dumps` and `loads`](../security/signing.md)).

`Signer` takes keyword arguments only: positional ones, deprecated in 4.2, were removed in 5.1 (`docs/releases/5.1.txt`), and `TimestampSigner` inherits the same `__init__` (`django/core/signing.py:Signer.__init__`).

`Signer` takes keyword arguments only: positional ones, deprecated in 4.2, were removed in 5.1 (`docs/releases/5.1.txt`), and `TimestampSigner` inherits the same `__init__` (`django/core/signing.py:Signer.__init__`).
It came in 4.1, when `CsrfViewMiddleware` stopped masking the secret in its cookie, to keep it masked while a project's instances were upgraded (`docs/releases/4.1.txt`).

Nothing at this commit reads it: under 5.2.17 and every later release a project that sets it true gets, without a warning, a cookie of 32 characters, the secret itself (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._set_csrf_cookie`).

A cookie of 64, a masked secret, is still accepted, and unmasked as it is read (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._get_secret`; [The CSRF secret and its token](../security/csrf-token.md)).
